A_target.statement:
Let $F: \R^n \times \R^m \to \R^m$ be [[Definition:Continuously Differentiable|continuously differentiable]] with $\map F {a, b} = 0$ and $\map {D_y F} {a, b}$ [[Definition:Invertible Matrix|invertible]].
Then there exist neighborhoods $U \ni a$, $V \ni b$ and a [[Definition:Continuously Differentiable|continuously differentiable]] $g: U \to V$ such that:
:$\forall x \in U: \map F {x, \map g x} = 0$

B_source.statement:
Let $\struct {X, d}$ be a [[Definition:Complete Metric Space|complete metric space]] and $T: X \to X$ a [[Definition:Contraction Mapping|contraction]].
Then $T$ has a [[Definition:Unique|unique]] [[Definition:Fixed Point|fixed point]].

substitutions.complete metric space X: a closed ball of candidate y-values (continuous functions of x)

derived.contraction constant < 1: smallness from invertibility and continuity near (a,b)

object_map.reformulation: Recast F(x,y)=0 as a fixed-point equation y = T(y) by a Newton-like correction using the inverse y-derivative.

validity_conditions: D_y F(a,b) is invertible, so T(y) = y - [D_y F(a,b)]^{-1} F(x,y) is well-defined and has a fixed point exactly where F(x,y)=0.
Continuity of DF near (a,b) makes T a contraction on a small closed ball (complete), so Banach applies.
The unique fixed point depends smoothly on x, giving the implicit function y(x).
proof_plan:
Let $L = \map {D_y F} {a, b}$ and define:
:$\map {T_x} y = y - L^{-1} \map F {x, y}$
Then $\map {T_x} y = y \iff \map F {x, y} = 0$.

$\map {D_y T_x} y = I - L^{-1} \map {D_y F} {x, y}$, which is small near $\tuple {a, b}$ by [[Definition:Continuous Mapping|continuity]].
On a small closed ball $\overline {\map {B_r} b}$ and for $x$ near $a$, $T_x$ maps the ball into itself with $\norm {\map {D_y T_x} y} \le \dfrac 1 2$.
By the [[Mean Value Inequality]], $T_x$ is a [[Definition:Contraction Mapping|contraction]].

The closed ball is [[Definition:Complete Metric Space|complete]].
By the [[Banach Fixed-Point Theorem]], $T_x$ has a unique fixed point $\map g x$ for each $x \in U$.

The fixed point depends continuously on $x$, as the contraction constant is uniform.
Differentiating $\map F {x, \map g x} = 0$ gives:
:$\map {D g} x = -\map {D_y F} {x, \map g x}^{-1} \map {D_x F} {x, \map g x}$
so $g$ is continuously differentiable, which is the [[Implicit Function Theorem]].
{{qed}}
